derivation.title: Rigorous Derivation
derivation.lead: We need only a little: the ideal gas equation as a starting point, the idea of a molecule as a finite-sized sphere, and one consideration that a molecule near the wall is not surrounded by neighbors on all sides. Everything else is arithmetic and two derivatives.

steps.text: First, let's measure how big the problem is. Take one mole of carbon dioxide at 20 °C and calculate the ratio $Z = pV/(nRT)$. For an ideal gas, it is identically equal to one at any pressure — that's the whole point of the equation of state. Experiment gives something different: at one atmosphere $Z \approx 0.995$, at ten bars about 0.94, at forty about 0.73. The first deviation can be blamed on instruments, the second no longer can, the third is a quarter of the value. Moreover, its sign is definite: the gas occupies a smaller volume than an ideal gas should, meaning something pulls molecules toward each other. And at very high pressures, $Z$ for all gases exceeds one — then the gas occupies a volume larger than it should, meaning something prevents molecules from approaching. Hence the plan: two corrections, of different signs.
steps.figCaption: Compressibility factor of carbon dioxide at 20 °C: ideal gas is a horizontal line at one, real gas dips down and by forty bars loses a quarter

steps.text: The first correction is for the finite volume of molecules. Let the molecule be not a point but a hard sphere of diameter $d$. Then the centers of two molecules cannot come closer than $d$: around the center of each there is a forbidden sphere of radius $d$, into which the center of a neighbor cannot enter. The volume of this forbidden sphere is $\tfrac{4}{3}\pi d^{3}$, and the volume of the molecule itself is $\tfrac{4}{3}\pi (d/2)^{3}$: the radius is half as large, so the volume is eight times smaller. The forbidden volume is eight times the molecule's volume — but it is shared by a pair, and we cannot attribute it entirely to each of the two, otherwise we would count the same prohibition twice. Divide in half: per molecule there are four of its own volumes, and the free space for motion is $V - nb$. Let's check the correction in reverse — this is more reliable than checking it by itself. From experimental isotherms of carbon dioxide, fitting gives $b = 42.7$ cm³/mol; hence the volume of one molecule $v = b/(4N_A) = 1.77\cdot10^{-29}$ m³, then $d^{3} = 6v/\pi = 3.39\cdot10^{-29}$ m³ and $d = 3.24$ Å. The reference kinetic diameter of the CO$_2$ molecule is 3.3 Å, and it was obtained from a completely different experiment, from viscosity and diffusion. The error is two percent: so $b$ is not a fitting patch, but indeed the size of the molecule.
steps.latex: v_{\text{excl}}^{\text{pair}} = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi d^{3} = 8\,v_{\text{mol}}, \quad b = \tfrac{1}{2}N_A\cdot 8 v_{\text{mol}} = 4 N_A v_{\text{mol}} \;\Longrightarrow\; d = \sqrt[3]{\frac{3b}{2\pi N_A}} = 3.24\ \text{Å}
steps.figCaption: Centers of two spheres do not come closer than a diameter: the forbidden sphere of radius d is twice as wide as the molecule and therefore eight times its volume, and each molecule gets half of this prohibition

steps.text: The second correction is for attraction. A molecule deep inside the gas is surrounded by neighbors on all sides, and their attraction on average cancels out: as much pulls to the right, so much to the left. A molecule approaching the wall has no neighbors ahead — only behind. They slow it down, and it hits the wall more weakly than an ideal gas molecule would. So the manometer will show a pressure lower than the purely kinetic one by some amount $\Delta p$. Let's estimate what this quantity depends on. First, on how many molecules hit the wall per second — and this is proportional to the density $n/V$. Second, on how strongly each is pulled back — and this is proportional to the number of pulling neighbors, i.e., the same density $n/V$. Two densities multiply, and we get a square. Note what is absent from this reasoning: no details about the nature of attraction. It only needs to exist and act at short distances.
steps.latex: \Delta p \ \propto\ \underbrace{\frac{n}{V}}_{\text{how many hit}} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{n}{V}}_{\text{how many pull}} \;\Longrightarrow\; \Delta p = a\,\frac{n^{2}}{V^{2}}
steps.figCaption: Deep in the gas, attraction from neighbors cancels in all directions; near the wall, neighbors remain only behind, and the molecule hits more weakly

steps.text: Now assemble. In the ideal gas equation, we replace the volume with the free volume, and to the measured pressure we add what attraction took away — we get the van der Waals equation. Let's check it in three ways. Dimensions: $[b] = $ m³/mol, so that $nb$ is a volume; $[a] = $ Pa·m⁶/mol², so that $an^2/V^2$ is a pressure. Limit transition: as $V \to \infty$, both corrections vanish, and exactly $pV = nRT$ remains — as it should be for a rarefied gas. Order of magnitude at normal conditions (one mole occupies 22.41 liters): $nb/V = 42.7/22,410 = 0.19\%$, and $an^2/V^2 = 0.3640/0.02241^{2} = 725$ Pa, i.e., 0.72 percent of an atmosphere. Both corrections are less than a percent — that's why the ideal gas satisfied everyone for so long and continues to satisfy in most calculations.
steps.figCaption: Two corrections in their places: to the pressure is added what attraction took away, from the volume is subtracted what the molecules themselves occupied

steps.text: Now let's see what the equation says about the shape of isotherms. Fix $T$ and solve the equation for $V$: after multiplying by $V^{2}$, it becomes cubic, meaning at a given pressure there can be either one root or three. This is already a hint. At high temperature, the curve $p(V)$ decreases monotonically and is almost indistinguishable from the hyperbola of an ideal gas. At low temperature, a hump appears: a section where pressure increases with volume. Physically this is impossible, and not just 'because it's strange', but for a specific reason. Suppose a densification randomly arises in such a medium. A reduced volume here means reduced pressure, neighboring matter rushes in, the densification grows, pressure drops even more. There is no restoring force at any stage — the state is mechanically unstable and simply does not occur.
steps.latex: pV^{3} - (pb + RT)\,V^{2} + aV - ab = 0 \qquad (n = 1), \qquad \text{forbidden: } \left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial V}\right)_T > 0
steps.figCaption: Three isotherms: above the critical temperature the curve is monotonic, below it has a hump, and the section with increasing pressure at increasing volume is mechanically impossible

steps.text: What is actually there? Andrews' experiment answers: instead of a hump, a strictly horizontal plateau. While the plateau lasts, compression does not change pressure at all; something else changes — the fraction of liquid grows, the fraction of vapor decreases, and at one end of the plateau the substance is entirely vapor, at the other entirely liquid. The height of the plateau, however, cannot be arbitrary. Maxwell noticed that if you draw it in the wrong place, then going along the plateau in one direction and along the van der Waals curve back, we would return to the initial state, having obtained nonzero work at a single temperature. That cannot happen. So the work along a closed path is zero, and this exactly means that the plateau cuts off equal areas from the hump and the trough.
steps.figCaption: Maxwell's equal-area rule: the horizontal line is drawn so that the shaded areas above and below it match — only then the work along a closed path is zero

steps.text: The higher the temperature, the shorter the plateau: liquid and vapor differ less and less. At a certain temperature, the hump and trough merge into a single point, the plateau shrinks to zero, and the difference between liquid and vapor disappears completely. Mathematically, at this point the tangent is horizontal and simultaneously the curve changes the sign of curvature — that is, both the first and second derivatives of pressure with respect to volume at constant temperature vanish. The first condition gives $RT/(V-b)^{2} = 2a/V^{3}$, the second — $RT/(V-b)^{3} = 3a/V^{4}$. Dividing the first by the second, we get $V - b = 2V/3$, i.e., $V_c = 3b$; substituting this into the first condition, we find $RT_c = 8a/(27b)$, and substituting both into the equation of state itself — $p_c = a/(27b^{2})$. Now the numbers. For carbon dioxide ($a = 3.640$ l²·bar/mol², $b = 42.67$ cm³/mol) we get 304.0 K and 74.0 bar versus measured 304.13 K and 73.77 bar — an error of 0.04 and 0.4 percent. For water ($a = 5.536$, $b = 30.49$) we get 647.0 K and 220.6 bar versus 647.10 K and 220.64 bar, i.e., the same 374 °C and 218 atmospheres that in the topic on phase transitions are called the limit of applicability of the boiling curve. For nitrogen 126.2 K and 33.9 bar versus 126.2 and 34.0, for helium 5.18 K and 2.26 bar versus 5.19 and 2.27. Four substances, critical temperatures spread over a factor of one hundred twenty, error — fractions of a percent.
steps.latex: \left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial V}\right)_T = -\frac{RT}{(V-b)^{2}} + \frac{2a}{V^{3}} = 0, \quad \left(\frac{\partial^{2} p}{\partial V^{2}}\right)_T = \frac{2RT}{(V-b)^{3}} - \frac{6a}{V^{4}} = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; V_c = 3b,\ \ T_c = \frac{8a}{27Rb},\ \ p_c = \frac{a}{27b^{2}}
steps.figCaption: The critical point is where the maximum and minimum of the isotherm merge: the tangent is horizontal, and simultaneously the curvature changes sign, and from these two conditions all three coordinates drop out

steps.text: The main consequence and the main honest test remain. Above the critical temperature, the cubic equation at any pressure has exactly one root: no plateau, no coexistence, no meniscus forms. Compress as much as you like — the substance will smoothly thicken until it becomes denser than water, but you will never see a phase boundary. This is exactly what it means that above $T_c$ a gas cannot be liquefied by any pressure, and this is what Andrews saw for carbon dioxide above 31 °C. And the test is this. From the three critical coordinates, form a dimensionless combination $Z_c = p_cV_c/(RT_c)$. The constants $a$ and $b$ cancel completely, and a pure number $3/8 = 0.375$ remains — the same for all substances in the world. This is no longer a fit, but a prediction, and it can only be confirmed or refuted. Experiment: 0.274 for carbon dioxide, 0.229 for water, 0.289 for nitrogen, 0.301 for helium. None equals 0.375. The model misses by a third, and the error lies entirely in the volume: $V_c = 3b$ gives for CO$_2$ 128 cm³/mol versus measured 94.
steps.figCaption: Above the critical temperature there is no plateau at any pressure: the substance thickens continuously, and the boundary between liquid and gas does not appear at all

derivation.plateCap: Two corrections to the ideal gas and no more. On the left in parentheses is the pressure that would be if molecules did not attract; on the right in parentheses is the volume that remains for them to move. All the unexpected reward — isotherms with a hump, coexistence plateau, critical point, and the law of corresponding states — is obtained from these two corrections and two derivatives.
derivation.note: Let's list what we assumed along the way. First: molecules are hard spheres. The real repulsive potential is not a vertical wall but a steep slope, and the 'diameter' of a molecule therefore depends on the energy with which it hits, i.e., on temperature. Second, and this is heavier: we replaced attraction with an average. Each molecule in our model feels not specific neighbors, but a uniform field created by the average density. This approximation is called the mean-field approximation, and it breaks down exactly where it is most interesting — near the critical point, where density fluctuates in large patches. Third: $a$ and $b$ are considered constants, independent of both temperature and density. Fourth: we did not distinguish between different molecules anywhere, i.e., the equation is written for a pure substance, not a mixture. Fifth: we did not prove the equal-area rule, but justified it by the consideration of work along a closed path; a rigorous proof goes through the equality of chemical potentials of phases and belongs to Gibbs thermodynamics. Finally, it is worth calling things by their names: this is not a derivation from first principles, but a correction of a known equation by two reasonable terms. Its value is not in accuracy — accuracy, as we saw, is moderate — but in that it predicts from almost nothing the existence of the critical point, which before it no one could explain.

math.title: The Math Needed Here
math.lead: Three topics: how to estimate, which correction is currently more important, why the derivative needs a subscript, and how the integral uniquely sets the height of the plateau.

items.why: There are two corrections, and they pull $Z$ in opposite directions: the finite volume makes $Z$ greater than one, while attraction makes it less. Who wins is clear from an expansion in small density. We expand the equation in powers of $1/V_m$ and keep the first term: $Z \approx 1 + (b - a/RT)/V_m$. Everything is decided by the bracket. If $a/RT > b$, i.e., at low temperatures, attraction wins and $Z < 1$ — exactly what we saw for carbon dioxide. If the temperature is high, the bracket is positive and the gas is 'stiffer' than an ideal gas. Right at the boundary, at $T = a/(Rb)$, the corrections cancel each other out, and the real gas is indistinguishable from an ideal gas over a wide range of pressures: this temperature is called the Boyle temperature. For van der Waals, it equals $\tfrac{27}{8}T_c$, i.e., 1026 K for CO$_2$ and 426 K for nitrogen, while measured values are about 714 and 327 K. The overestimate by a third for nitrogen and almost 1.5 times for carbon dioxide is the same order of inaccuracy as for $Z_c$, and this is no coincidence: both quantities test the model where it is no longer quantitative.

In the critical point condition, it is not $dp/dV$ but $(\partial p/\partial V)_T$, and the subscript is essential, not decorative. Pressure depends on two variables at once, and a 'derivative with respect to volume' without specifying what happens to the second variable is simply undefined: along an isotherm you get one number, along an adiabat another, and along an isochore the question makes no sense. We fix the temperature because the isotherm is exactly what Andrews's experiment plots. Next, we count equations and unknowns. There are three unknowns: $V_c$, $T_c$, $p_c$. There are also three equations: the equation of state itself plus two conditions on the derivatives. The system is closed, and therefore the critical point is uniquely determined, without any additional knowledge about the substance.
items.latex: \left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial V}\right)_T = 0, \qquad \left(\frac{\partial^{2} p}{\partial V^{2}}\right)_T = 0, \qquad p = p(V_c, T_c)

items.what: The integral that puts the plateau in its place
items.why: The equal-area rule looks geometric, but it is computed analytically, and for van der Waals the integral is fully evaluated in elementary functions. We need $\int p\,dV$ along the isotherm; the first term gives a logarithm, the second gives one over volume. Equating the area under the straight plateau to the area under the curve gives one equation relating the saturation pressure to the two volumes. Two more equations give the equalities $p(V_l) = p(V_g) = p_{\text{sat}}$. Three equations, three unknowns — the problem is solved numerically, and that is exactly what the stand does when it draws the coexistence dome. It is useful to note that the same integral is work: the equality of areas means zero work over a closed isothermal path, and a nonzero value would imply a machine extracting work from a single heat reservoir.
items.latex: \int p\,dV = RT\ln(V-b) + \frac{a}{V} \;\Longrightarrow\; p_{\text{sat}}(V_g - V_l) = RT\ln\frac{V_g - b}{V_l - b} + \frac{a}{V_g} - \frac{a}{V_l}

example.title: Example with numbers
example.lead: Let's calculate the critical point of carbon dioxide using two tabulated constants and check the answer against the red fire extinguisher cylinder that stands in any corridor.
example.given: For carbon dioxide, $a = 3.640$ L²·bar/mol², $b = 0.04267$ L/mol. The gas constant in these units is $R = 0.083145$ L·bar/(mol·K). Find $T_c$, $p_c$, $V_c$, and the dimensionless ratio $Z_c$; compare with the measured values 304.13 K, 73.8 bar, and 94 cm³/mol.
example.law: $V_c = 3b$, $T_c = 8a/(27Rb)$, $p_c = a/(27b^{2})$ — three formulas obtained from the condition that the maximum and minimum of the isotherm merge.

solution.text: Temperature. The denominator is a product of three numbers; we calculate it first to avoid losing the order of magnitude.
Pressure. Here $b$ is squared, so an error in $b$ enters doubled — this is worth remembering when making estimates.
Volume — the simplest formula and, as will become clear, the most unsuccessful.
Dimensionless check. We calculate it in two ways: by the formula $3/8$ and by substituting the measured numbers. The discrepancy is the price of the model.

We bring the misses together and see where exactly the error lives. The temperature missed by 0.04 percent, the pressure by 0.4, the volume by 36. The ratio $0.375/0.274 = 1.37$ coincides with the ratio $128.1/94 = 1.36$ — meaning all the inaccuracy in $Z_c$ is the inaccuracy in $V_c$, and nothing else.

example.answer: The critical point of carbon dioxide: 304 K, that is 31 °C, at 74 bar. Temperature and pressure are predicted to within fractions of a percent; the critical volume is overestimated by a third.
example.check: Is this reasonable and what follows from it? Thirty-one degrees is room temperature, and here is a direct consequence. In a fire extinguisher at 20 °C, that is, below the critical point, carbon dioxide is on the coexistence plateau: inside there is liquid and vapor, the pressure is 57 bar, and it does not depend on how much substance remains — that is why there is no pressure gauge on a CO2 fire extinguisher; it is weighed. Let's check the mass. The density of liquid carbon dioxide at 20 °C is about 0.77 kg per liter, and the standard filling of cylinders is 0.75 kg per liter. So the cylinder is filled with liquid almost to the top, leaving only a few percent for expansion, and such stinginess of the reserve requires an explanation: it means that heating the cylinder is absolutely forbidden. Take the same extinguisher out into the sun — and trouble will come before the critical point. The filling density of 0.75 kg/L is higher than the critical density of carbon dioxide, which is calculated from the already obtained $V_c$: 44 g/mol per 94 cm³/mol gives 0.47 kg/L. So when heated, it is not the liquid that disappears, but the vapor: the liquid expands, eats the vapor bubble, and already around 22 °C fills the cylinder completely. Further expansion is impossible, the walls are rigid, and the liquid is almost incompressible — and the pressure grows not by percentages, but by factors — long before the thermometer reaches 31 °C. That is why a rupture disc is installed on the cylinder, and it must be stored in a cool place. The second consequence is checked in the opposite direction: for oxygen and nitrogen, the critical temperatures are 155 and 126 K, far below room temperature, and in cylinders they are always gas — no matter how much you compress. If your calculation gave a critical temperature of a hundred kelvins or a thousand for carbon dioxide, look for the lost 27 in the denominator or degrees Celsius instead of kelvins.

constants.title: Constants of this section
constants.lead: Five numbers: one universal constant, two tabulated substance constants, one practically important critical point, and one dimensionless number that catches the model in inaccuracy.

items.name: Universal gas constant
items.why: Since 2019 it is not measured but calculated exactly: $R = N_A k_B$, and both quantities are fixed numbers by the new SI definition. In real gas calculations other units are also convenient: 0.083145 L·bar/(mol·K) — then volumes are in liters and pressures in bars, and in critical point formulas you don't have to juggle powers of ten.
items.mnemo: Eight and three tenths. From this immediately the molar volume at normal conditions: $22.4 = 8.314\cdot 273/101\,325\cdot 1000$ liters.

items.name: Attraction constant of carbon dioxide
items.why: A measure of how strongly molecules attract each other, and its spread across substances is huge: helium 0.00346, nitrogen 0.1370, carbon dioxide 0.3640, water 0.5536 — a factor of one hundred sixty from edge to edge. The order of this series reads directly: an inert single atom, a nonpolar molecule, a molecule with a strong quadrupole moment, a molecule with hydrogen bonds. It is $a$ that is responsible for water being liquid at room temperature, while nitrogen is a gas at the same temperature.
items.mnemo: Look at $a$ as the liquefaction temperature: $T_c = 8a/(27Rb)$, and since $b$ is of the same order for all, the critical temperature goes almost proportionally to $a$.

items.name: Co-volume constant of carbon dioxide
items.why: The spread here is incomparably smaller than for $a$: helium 23.8, water 30.5, nitrogen 38.7, carbon dioxide 42.7 cm³/mol — only a factor of two from edge to edge, because all molecules are roughly the same size, and size enters cubed. A useful reading of this number: 42.7 cm³/mol is four times the total volume of the molecules themselves, so the co-volume of a mole of carbon dioxide is about 10.7 cm³. Compare with the 22,400 cm³ that a mole occupies in gas: molecules fill five hundredths of a percent of the space provided.
items.mnemo: $b$ is approximately equal to the molar volume of the substance in liquid form: for carbon dioxide the liquid gives 57 cm³/mol at 20 °C — the same order. This is not a coincidence: in a liquid molecules are just as crowded.

items.name: Critical point of water
items.why: The number around which all thermal power engineering is built. A conventional steam boiler operates with a drum where boiling water is separated from steam — but above the critical point boiling does not exist, there is nothing to separate, and the drum is not needed at all. Supercritical power units operate at 24–25 MPa and 540–600 °C, ultra-supercritical ones at 30 MPa and above. The gain is direct: the higher the temperature of the working fluid, the higher the limiting efficiency, and crossing the critical point raised the efficiency of coal plants from about 38 to 45 percent. In the topic on phase transitions, this same point is called the boundary beyond which the boiling curve simply ends.
items.mnemo: 374 degrees and 218 atmospheres. Keep in mind as "two hundred times above the atmosphere and twice as hot as boiling water" — both halves are easy to remember.

items.name: Critical compressibility factor
items.value: 3/8 = 0.375 according to van der Waals; 0.229 for water, 0.274 for CO₂, 0.289 for nitrogen, 0.301 for helium
items.why: The absence of units is not a trifle here, but the whole point. Since the quantity is dimensionless, $a$ and $b$ cancel out, i.e., all information about the specific substance disappears; only a pure prediction of the model remains, which cannot be adjusted. Experiment gives numbers noticeably less than 3/8. The spread between substances is also real, but tiny against the spread of constants: $Z_c$ varies from 0.23 to 0.30, i.e., by a third, while the $a$ themselves vary by a factor of one hundred sixty. Later equations of state fixed exactly this indicator: Redlich and Kwong in 1949 obtained 1/3, Peng and Robinson in 1976 — 0.307, which is already close to the measured value.
items.mnemo: Three eighths is the only number in the entire section that does not depend on either the substance or the units. That is why it serves as a verdict for the model.

synthesis.title: How This Connects to the Rest of the Course
synthesis.lead: This section sits exactly between two major topics: it takes the ideal gas and breaks it with two corrections, and the resulting break explains what thermodynamics previously took from experience.

items.h: Ideal Gas: Where We Came From
items.text: The equation $pV = nRT$ is derived in the topic on molecular structure from collisions of point molecules with the wall, and there you can also see what is missing from that derivation: the size of molecules and the forces between them. We brought both back and got the critical point as a reward. Notice the direction of dependence: a real gas is not a 'different law' but the same one with two additions, and as $V \to \infty$, the additions vanish. This is how almost any extension of a theory works—the new must contain the old as a limiting case.

items.h: Phase Transitions: What We Gave a Foundation
items.text: In the topic on phase transitions, the boiling curve and the Clausius–Clapeyron equation describe the equilibrium of liquid and vapor, but the very existence of such equilibrium is taken as a given from experience. Here it emerged: the plateau on the isotherm is the coexistence of phases, and its ends are the densities of the liquid and saturated vapor. There, the critical point of water was called the boundary where the boiling curve ends—and now it is clear why: the ends of the plateau converge, the difference between phases disappears, and there is no boundary left to pass.

The correction $a$ says nothing about the origin of attraction—it is enough that it exists. That origin is analyzed in statistical physics: even for neutral nonpolar molecules, instantaneous fluctuations of the electron cloud induce a dipole in a neighbor, and an attraction arises that decays as the sixth power of distance. These forces bear the name van der Waals—after the same equation, not the other way around. From there also comes the explanation of why at high temperatures attraction stops interfering: the energy of thermal motion overcomes the energy of attraction, and molecules fly apart before they can stick together.

The second section will deal with the surface. That very force, which we here folded into a single constant $a$, is uncompensated at the boundary of a liquid—and from this grow surface tension, droplets, menisci, and the rise of water in capillaries. Incidentally, it becomes clear why surface tension vanishes at the critical point: the boundary between phases itself disappears, and with it the cost for it. The third section will address heat capacities and also show that for a real gas the familiar relation $C_p - C_V = R$ ceases to be exact—the same two corrections are to blame.

items.h: Liquefaction of Gases: Where This Works
items.text: The critical temperature is the first thing a cryogenic engineer looks at. Carbon dioxide at room temperature is liquefied by simple compression; air is not, and no compressor will help here: you must first cool it below 132 K. Cooling is done by Joule–Thomson throttling, that is, releasing compressed gas through a narrow orifice; it works precisely because of the correction $a$ and is therefore impossible for an ideal gas. The derivation of this effect does not fit into our section, and we state it here as a fact. This same ladder was climbed historically: air in 1895, hydrogen in 1898, helium in 1908—and each next gas required being pre-cooled by the previous one.

curiosities.title: Fun: check it with your own hands
curiosities.lead: Both van der Waals corrections can be felt in the kitchen in five minutes, literally: one is felt with the palm, the other is seen through plastic.

items.h: Two syringes: air compresses, water does not
items.text: Take two identical syringes without needles, about twenty milliliters. Fill the first with air, the second with water, completely, so that no bubbles remain. Close the nozzle tightly with your finger and press the plunger. The air plunger will easily move halfway. The water plunger will not move at all, no matter how hard you push. Before reading further, try to estimate how many times harder you would have to press to compress water even by one percent.
items.answer: Let's calculate. To compress air by half, you need to raise the pressure to two atmospheres, i.e., add one atmosphere. With a plunger diameter of 20 mm, its area is 3.1 cm², and the required force comes out to about 32 newtons — three kilograms, exactly what the palm feels. Now water. Its bulk modulus is 2.2 GPa: to reduce the volume by one percent, you need 22 MPa, i.e., 220 atmospheres, and that on the same plunger is about seven hundred kilograms. You will crush the syringe before you compress the water by a noticeable amount. This is the correction $b$ in its pure form. In a gas, molecules occupy five hundredths of a percent of the volume, and compressing almost empty space is easy. In a liquid, they are packed tightly, there is practically no free volume, and the resistance to compression is set not by the motion of molecules, but by the repulsion of their electron shells. The van der Waals equation is remarkable precisely because it describes both limits with one formula: at large $V$, $nRT/V$ works, and as $V$ approaches $nb$, the denominator goes to zero and the pressure shoots up vertically.

items.h: A transparent lighter as a pressure gauge
items.text: Take an ordinary lighter with a transparent body and look through it. Inside there is liquid, above it a seemingly empty space — that is vapor. No need to light anything: the experiment is done by looking. Squeeze the lighter in your fist for a minute, warm it to body temperature, and look again. The liquid level has barely changed. Now the question: has the pressure inside increased or not, and if it has, why didn't the liquid all boil away at once?
items.answer: The pressure increased, and noticeably. In the lighter there is butane; its saturated vapor pressure at 20 °C is about 2 bar, and at 35 °C already about 3.3 bar — a one-and-a-half-fold increase from just the warmth of the palm. And the liquid did not boil away because you are exactly on the coexistence plateau, which we derived in step six. On the plateau, the pressure is set solely by temperature and does not depend on how much liquid and how much vapor there is. Exactly as many molecules evaporated as needed to raise the vapor pressure to the new equilibrium value — and that is a fraction of a percent of the contents. That is why there is no pressure gauge in a lighter and why it burns the same until it is almost empty: as long as there is liquid inside, the outlet pressure is constant. Also note where you are on the diagram: the critical temperature of butane is 425 K, i.e., 152 °C, and you are working at 293–308 K. This is deep under the coexistence dome, near its base. If the critical temperature of butane were below room temperature, like nitrogen, there would be no liquid in the lighter at all — only compressed gas, and it would run out after a dozen presses.

items.h: Why oxygen in a cylinder is a gas, but carbon dioxide in a cylinder is a liquid
items.text: A medical oxygen cylinder holds 150 bar, and all the while inside is gas. A carbon dioxide fire extinguisher holds only 57 bar — and inside is liquid. Less pressure, yet the substance is liquefied. How is that possible?
items.answer: Pressure is irrelevant here; temperature decides. Oxygen has a critical temperature of 155 K, i.e., minus 118 °C. At room temperature of twenty degrees, you are twice above it on the absolute scale, where no coexistence plateau exists at any pressure: compress to a thousand atmospheres — you get a very dense gas and not a drop of liquid. Carbon dioxide has a critical temperature of 304 K, i.e., plus 31 °C, and room temperature of twenty degrees lies below it. So the plateau exists, and as soon as you raise the pressure to 57 bar, the substance hits it and begins to liquefy. Hence the difference in handling the cylinders. An oxygen cylinder can be weighed or measured with a pressure gauge — the pressure honestly drops as it is consumed. Measuring a carbon dioxide cylinder with a gauge is useless: as long as there is any liquid left inside, the pressure stays at those same 57 bar, and you can only know the remainder by weighing. The same logic applies to liquefied gases in general: propane in a country cylinder is liquid because its critical temperature is 370 K, while methane in a car cylinder is gas because its critical temperature is 191 K.

items.text: Right above the critical point, a substance becomes a supercritical fluid: its density is almost liquid-like, while its viscosity and ability to penetrate are almost gas-like. For carbon dioxide, the threshold is ridiculously accessible: 31 °C and 74 bar. A whole industry is built on this. Supercritical CO$_2$ washes caffeine out of green coffee beans, hop resins from cones, essential oils from plants, and after pressure release simply evaporates, leaving no solvent traces — previously dichloromethane was used instead. It is also used to clean precision optics and process semiconductor wafers.
items.answer: There is also a spectacle at the critical point worth seeing at least once on video. Approach it closely in temperature — and the transparent substance suddenly becomes turbid to milky opacity, and then, a little to the side, clears again. This is critical opalescence, and it is a direct refutation of our own approximation. We assumed that each molecule feels a uniform average field of neighbors. At the critical point, the density difference between liquid and vapor goes to zero, and with it the cost of density fluctuations disappears: it costs almost nothing to densify or rarefy the substance. Therefore, density patches of the size of the wavelength of light appear in it, and they scatter light in all directions — like milk or fog. Van der Waals could not explain this: scattering on density fluctuations was worked out by Marian Smoluchowski in 1908 and Einstein in 1910, and the Dutchmen Ornstein and Zernike in 1914 added correlations of neighboring patches to the picture — exactly what the mean field lacks. A quantitative theory came even later: the exponents with which densities diverge at the critical point turned out to be the same for completely different substances and even for magnets, and the explanation of this universality is a separate big story, to which Landau and Wilson contributed.

items.h: Where the model lies most — and why it is useful to know
items.text: It is natural to assume that the equation works worst where the gas is dense. In fact, it works worst at a single point — the critical one — and precisely where it looks like a triumph.
items.answer: Let's examine this honestly. In temperature and pressure, the critical point is predicted with an accuracy of fractions of a percent, and that is a genuine success. In volume, it misses by a third, and that is not accidental: it is systematic and in one direction for all substances. The reason is the mean-field approximation. Near the critical point, density fluctuates in huge patches, and the "average density" with which we replaced specific neighbors ceases to describe anything. Numerically, this is seen in the exponent. Van der Waals predicts that the density difference between liquid and vapor goes to zero as the square root of the temperature deficit, i.e., with exponent 1/2. Experiment gives 0.326, and this number is the same for carbon dioxide, water, xenon, and even for the magnetization of iron at the Curie point. The coincidence of exponents in such different systems is called universality; Landau's theory dealt with it, and the final calculation was given by the renormalization group in the seventies. The practical conclusion from all this is simple and useful: the van der Waals equation is excellent for estimating where a substance liquefies at all and what order of pressures are needed, but engineering tables are never calculated with it. For tables, Peng–Robinson equations or direct measurements are used.

blocks.h: Constants $a$ and $b$ are not really constant
blocks.text: We treated them as if they were passport data of a substance, and this is the main arithmetic weakness of the model. The repulsion between molecules is not a vertical wall but a very steep slope, so the effective diameter depends on the energy with which molecules collide with each other, that is, on temperature: hot molecules are 'smaller'. Attraction also cannot be reduced to a single number — for polar molecules, dipole-dipole forces add to dispersion forces, for water, hydrogen bonds on top of everything, and their relative contribution changes with temperature in different ways. A systematic way to avoid such simplification is known: expand $Z$ in a series in density, and then the coefficients of the series — the virial ones — will themselves be functions of temperature, and the second of them is honestly calculated from the interaction potential. The van der Waals equation in this language is a rough approximation with $B(T) = b - a/RT$, and it is clear what is rough about it: the real $B(T)$ is not described by such a simple formula.

blocks.h: Mean field: why $Z_c$ misses by a third
blocks.text: The key assumption is hidden in the third step of the derivation: our molecule feels not specific neighbors but a uniform field created by the average density of the gas. As long as the gas is rarefied and homogeneous, this is reasonable. At the critical point, it is no longer: the substance there separates into large patches of density, and talking about 'average density' loses meaning exactly where we rely on it. Hence the miss in $V_c$ and the miss in the exponents with which quantities approach their critical values. It is useful to understand that the problem is not in the unfortunate form of the correction: any equation of state written in the mean field gives an exponent of 1/2 instead of the measured 0.326, no matter what terms are added to it. This is fixed not by selecting a formula but by a different language of description.

blocks.h: Metastable states: not the whole hump is equally forbidden
blocks.text: We said that the hump is replaced by a plateau, and this is true for equilibrium. But not the entire section on the hump is forbidden, only its middle — the one where $(\partial p/\partial V)_T > 0$. The curve connecting the points where the derivative vanishes is called the spinodal, and inside it there are indeed no states. But between the spinodal and the coexistence plateau lie metastable states: they are stable to small perturbations and therefore exist, sometimes for a long time. Superheated liquid is from this region: pure water in a smooth mug in a microwave heats above one hundred degrees and does not boil until a nucleation center appears, and then it boils all at once. Supersaturated vapor is from the same place; the Wilson cloud chamber worked on it, where a flying particle left a trail of droplets. Our model describes this region even qualitatively correctly, but where exactly the stability boundary passes, it predicts only approximately.

blocks.h: One substance, one phase, no chemistry
blocks.text: The equation is written for a pure substance. For a mixture, the constants have to be averaged according to empirical mixing rules, and these rules are a separate engineering science, without which no gas processing plant is calculated. Further: we nowhere allowed that molecules can combine. But they can — acetic acid in vapor is half composed of double molecules, and no $a$ and $b$ will describe that. Finally, the solid phase is absent from the model altogether: our isotherms know liquid and gas but do not know ice. Below the triple point, the equation continues to draw a liquid-vapor plateau where the substance in liquid form no longer exists. It is useful to keep the model's boundaries in mind as a list, not as a feeling: pure substance, two phases, no chemical transformations, temperature not too close to critical.

memo.essence: An ideal gas knows nothing of two things: that molecules take up space and that they attract each other. Restoring both — subtracting $nb$ from the volume and adding $an^{2}/V^{2}$ to the pressure — yields the van der Waals equation, and with it the isotherms with a hump, the coexistence plateau of liquid and vapor, and the critical point with coordinates $V_c = 3b$, $T_c = 8a/(27Rb)$, $p_c = a/(27b^{2})$. Above the critical temperature, there is no plateau at any pressure — the gas cannot be liquefied by compression.

keyIdeas.title: Two corrections, opposite signs
keyIdeas.text: The finite volume makes the gas stiffer than ideal, the attraction makes it softer. The larger one wins: $Z \approx 1 + (b - a/RT)/V_m$

keyIdeas.title: Fourfold, not threefold
keyIdeas.text: $b = 4N_A v_{\text{mol}}$: the forbidden sphere around a molecule is twice as wide as the molecule itself, hence eight times the volume, but it is shared by a pair

keyIdeas.title: Critical point from an inflection
keyIdeas.text: Two derivatives set to zero simultaneously give $V_c = 3b$, $T_c = 8a/(27Rb)$, $p_c = a/(27b^{2})$ — and no new fitting parameters

keyIdeas.title: 3/8 versus 0.27
keyIdeas.text: The dimensionless $Z_c$ cannot be tuned by anything, and experiment gives 0.23–0.30 instead of 0.375. The whole error sits in $V_c$, overestimated by a third

where: Fire extinguisher: carbon dioxide at 20 °C is below its critical point, so inside there is liquid under 57 bars, and the remainder is determined by weighing, not by a pressure gauge
Oxygen and methane cylinders: critical temperatures 155 and 191 K, room temperature is higher — inside there is always gas, no matter how much you compress
Supercritical power units: above 22.06 MPa and 374 °C there is no boiling, a drum separator is not needed, and the plant efficiency rises
Coffee decaffeination and extraction of hop resins: supercritical CO₂ at 31 °C and 74 bars, the solvent evaporates by itself
Air liquefaction: first cool below 132 K by throttling, and only then compress — the reverse order cannot be bypassed
memo.watchOut: Three pitfalls. The first is thinking that liquid is obtained by sufficient pressure: above the critical temperature no pressure helps, and this is not a matter of engineering but a matter of the absence of a plateau on the isotherm. The second is taking $b$ as the total volume of molecules: it is four times larger, and an estimate of the molecular size without this factor of four will miss by a factor of 1.6. The third is trusting the model quantitatively near the critical point: it gives temperature and pressure to within fractions of a percent, but volume and exponents with errors of tens of percent, because the mean-field approximation breaks down there.

quiz.q: At 20 °C, carbon dioxide liquefies already at 57 bar, while oxygen remains a gas even at 150 bar in a medical cylinder. What is the reason?
options: Room temperature is below the critical temperature for CO₂ (304 K) and much above the critical temperature for oxygen (155 K): above the critical temperature there is no coexistence plateau at any pressure
Oxygen molecules are lighter and attract each other more weakly, so it simply needs more pressure — about three hundred bar
Oxygen is chemically active, and active substances do not liquefy
It is a matter of cylinder strength: the walls could not withstand the pressure needed to liquefy oxygen
quiz.why: The ratio of the working temperature to the critical temperature decides, not the magnitude of pressure. Above $T_c$ the cubic equation has a single root at any $p$: the isotherm is monotonic, there is no horizontal plateau on it, hence there is no state in which liquid and vapor coexist. Compression gives an increasingly dense fluid, but the phase boundary never appears. The answer 'needs more pressure' looks plausible and is therefore dangerous: it assumes that liquefaction is a matter of sufficient effort, whereas it is a matter of fundamental impossibility. It is easy to check: liquid oxygen exists, but only below 155 K, and it is obtained by cooling, not by compression.
quiz.hint: Compare room temperature 293 K with the critical temperatures of both gases. What happens to the isotherm when the temperature is above the critical one?

quiz.q: On an isotherm below the critical one, the van der Waals equation gives a section where pressure increases with volume. What does this mean physically?
options: Such a state is mechanically unstable and cannot exist; in equilibrium the whole hump is replaced by a horizontal coexistence plateau of liquid and vapor
In this section the substance behaves like a solid, so ordinary reasoning does not apply
This is a consequence of a sign error in the attraction correction; the section must simply be discarded
Such states are realized if the substance is compressed slowly enough
quiz.why: If compression reduces pressure, then a random densification amplifies itself: in the densified place the pressure drops, the surrounding substance rushes in, the densification grows. There is no restoring force at any stage, and the state is not realized. In equilibrium, nature replaces the entire hump with a horizontal line, whose height is uniquely set by Maxwell's equal-area rule. The answer about slow compression is half wrong, and it is worth understanding where exactly: between the plateau and the spinodal — the line where the derivative vanishes — states do exist, they are metastable, these are superheated liquid and supersaturated vapor. But the section with positive derivative, which is asked about, is forbidden without any reservations.
quiz.hint: Imagine that in such a medium a small densification accidentally arises. What will happen to the pressure in it and where will the neighboring substance move afterwards?

quiz.q: In your own words: where does the correction $b$ come from and why is it four times the total volume of the molecules themselves, not equal to it?
quiz.why: A molecule is not a point but a sphere of diameter $d$, and the centers of two molecules cannot come closer than $d$. Therefore around the center of each there is a forbidden sphere of radius $d$, where the center of a neighbor cannot enter. The radius of this sphere is twice the radius of the molecule itself, and the volume is therefore eight times larger. But the prohibition applies to a pair of molecules at once, and attributing it entirely to each of the two would count the same prohibition twice. Dividing in half gives four own volumes per molecule, hence $b = 4N_A v_{\text{mol}}$. This is verified in reverse: from $b = 42.7$ cm³/mol for CO₂ it follows a diameter of 3.24 Å against the reference value of 3.3 Å.
quiz.hint: Draw two touching molecules and ask not 'how much space do the spheres occupy', but 'where can the center of a neighbor not go'. What radius does the forbidden region have and over how many molecules should it be divided?

quiz.q: For water, the van der Waals constant $b = 30.5$ cm³/mol. Estimate the diameter of a water molecule from it. Answer in angstroms (1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m).
quiz.why: From $b = 4N_A\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{6}d^{3}$ it follows that $d = \sqrt[3]{3b/(2\pi N_A)}$. We calculate: $3b = 91.5\cdot10^{-6}$ m³/mol, $2\pi N_A = 3.78\cdot10^{24}$ mol⁻¹, their ratio is $2.42\cdot10^{-29}$ m³, the cube root is $2.89\cdot10^{-10}$ m, that is 2.89 Å. Reference estimates of the water molecule size give 2.7–2.8 Å, so the estimate overestimates by about five percent — decent accuracy for a hard-sphere model. A useful sanity check: the water molecule must be smaller than the CO₂ molecule (3.24 Å by the same calculation), and indeed it is smaller.
quiz.hint: First find the volume of one molecule: divide $b$ by $4N_A$. Then recall that the volume of a sphere is $\tfrac{\pi}{6}d^{3}$, and take the cube root. Do not forget to convert cubic meters to cubic angstroms at the very end.

formula.name: Ecuación de Van der Waals
formula.alsoKnown: Ecuación de estado del gas real. Para un mol se escribe más corta: $(p + a/V_m^2)(V_m - b) = RT$, donde $V_m$ es el volumen molar

authors.what: selló un líquido en el cañón de un rifle junto con una bola y escuchó cómo rodaba; al calentar, el sonido del chapoteo desaparecía de repente: el límite del líquido se desvanecía. Esta fue la primera observación del fenómeno crítico, que nadie pudo explicar en ese entonces.

midió cuidadosamente las isotermas del dióxido de carbono y descubrió que por encima de 31 °C no se obtiene líquido a ninguna presión. También introdujo el término "punto crítico" y demostró que los estados gaseoso y líquido se transforman continuamente uno en otro, evitando ese punto.

en su tesis doctoral "Sobre la continuidad de los estados gaseoso y líquido" derivó la ecuación con dos correcciones y mostró que reproduce tanto las isotermas de Andrews como el punto crítico y la ley de los estados correspondientes. Premio Nobel de 1910.
demostró la regla de las áreas iguales, que determina de manera única la altura de la meseta de coexistencia; antes, esa altura tenía que tomarse de los experimentos.

formula.story: Van der Waals no era un hombre universitario. Hijo de un carpintero de Leiden, no había estudiado latín ni griego en la escuela, y sin ellos no se podía ingresar a una universidad holandesa; por eso enseñaba en una escuela y asistía a cursos como oyente libre, hasta que la ley de exámenes se flexibilizó. Defendió su tesis a los treinta y cinco años, en neerlandés, en un país que el mundo de la física apenas leía entonces. El trabajo fue notado por Maxwell: en 1874 lo analizó en la revista Nature y escribió que el nombre de van der Waals pronto estaría entre los primeros de la ciencia molecular. Luego la historia dio un giro inesperado. La consecuencia más práctica no fue la ecuación en sí, sino la ley de los estados correspondientes que se deriva de ella: si se miden la presión, el volumen y la temperatura en fracciones de los valores críticos, todos los gases se comportan igual. Heike Kamerlingh Onnes tomó esta ley como fórmula de diseño: a partir del comportamiento de los gases ya licuados, calculó qué esperar del helio y en 1908 obtuvo helio líquido a 4,2 K. Tres años después, al enfriar mercurio con ese helio, descubrió la superconductividad. La cadena que va desde un maestro de escuela que calculaba tamaños de moléculas hasta los imanes superconductores del tomógrafo resultó más corta de lo que parece.

derivation.title: Derivación rigurosa
derivation.lead: Se necesita poco: la ecuación del gas ideal como punto de partida, la idea de la molécula como una esfera de tamaño finito y una consideración sobre que la molécula cerca de la pared no está rodeada de vecinos por todos lados. Todo lo demás es aritmética y dos derivadas.

steps.text: Primero, midamos la magnitud del problema. Tomemos un mol de dióxido de carbono a 20 °C y calculemos la relación $Z = pV/(nRT)$. Para un gas ideal, es idénticamente igual a uno a cualquier presión; ese es todo el sentido de la ecuación de estado. La experiencia da otra cosa: a una atmósfera $Z \approx 0{,}995$, a diez bares alrededor de 0,94, a cuarenta aproximadamente 0,73. La primera desviación se puede atribuir a los instrumentos, la segunda ya no, la tercera es una cuarta parte de la magnitud. Además, su signo es definido: el gas ocupa un volumen menor que el que le correspondería a un gas ideal, es decir, algo atrae a las moléculas entre sí. Y a presiones muy altas, $Z$ para todos los gases supera la unidad; entonces el gas ocupa un volumen mayor que el debido, es decir, algo impide que las moléculas se acerquen. De ahí el plan: dos correcciones, de signos opuestos.
steps.figCaption: Coeficiente de compresibilidad del dióxido de carbono a 20 °C: el gas ideal es una línea horizontal en uno, el real desciende y a cuarenta bares pierde una cuarta parte

steps.text: La primera corrección es por el volumen propio. Supongamos que la molécula no es un punto, sino una esfera rígida de diámetro $d$. Entonces los centros de dos moléculas no pueden acercarse más que $d$: alrededor del centro de cada una hay una esfera prohibida de radio $d$, a la que el centro del vecino no tiene acceso. El volumen de esta esfera prohibida es $\tfrac{4}{3}\pi d^{3}$, y el volumen de la propia molécula es $\tfrac{4}{3}\pi (d/2)^{3}$: el radio es la mitad, por lo que el volumen es ocho veces menor. El volumen prohibido es ocho veces mayor que la molécula, pero es común a un par, y no se puede atribuir completamente a cada una de las dos, de lo contrario contaríamos la misma prohibición dos veces. Dividimos por la mitad: a cada molécula le corresponden cuatro de sus propios volúmenes, y el espacio libre para el movimiento es $V - nb$. Verifiquemos la corrección en sentido inverso: esto es más confiable que verificarla por sí misma. De las isotermas experimentales del dióxido de carbono, mediante ajuste se obtiene $b = 42{,}7$ cm³/mol; de aquí el volumen de una molécula $v = b/(4N_A) = 1{,}77\cdot10^{-29}$ m³, luego $d^{3} = 6v/\pi = 3{,}39\cdot10^{-29}$ m³ y $d = 3{,}24$ Å. El diámetro cinético de referencia de la molécula de CO$_2$ es 3,3 Å, y se obtuvo de un experimento completamente diferente, de la viscosidad y la difusión. El error es del dos por ciento: esto significa que $b$ no es un parche de ajuste, sino realmente el tamaño de la molécula.
steps.latex: v_{\text{excl}}^{\text{par}} = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi d^{3} = 8\,v_{\text{mol}}, \quad b = \tfrac{1}{2}N_A\cdot 8 v_{\text{mol}} = 4 N_A v_{\text{mol}} \;\Longrightarrow\; d = \sqrt[3]{\frac{3b}{2\pi N_A}} = 3{,}24\ \text{Å}
steps.figCaption: Los centros de dos esferas no se acercan más que un diámetro: la esfera prohibida de radio d es el doble de ancha que la molécula y, por tanto, ocho veces más voluminosa, y a cada molécula le corresponde la mitad de esta prohibición

steps.text: La segunda corrección es por la atracción. Una molécula en el interior del gas está rodeada de vecinos por todos lados, y su atracción en promedio se anula mutuamente: tanto tira hacia la derecha como hacia la izquierda. Una molécula que se acerca a la pared no tiene vecinos delante, solo detrás. Es frenada y golpea la pared con menos fuerza de la que golpearía un gas ideal. Por lo tanto, el manómetro mostrará una presión menor que la puramente cinética, en una cierta cantidad $\Delta p$. Estimemos de qué depende esta cantidad. Primero, de cuántas moléculas se acercan a la pared por segundo, lo cual es proporcional a la densidad $n/V$. Segundo, de cuán fuertemente es tirada hacia atrás cada una, lo cual es proporcional al número de vecinos que tiran, es decir, a la misma densidad $n/V$. Las dos densidades se multiplican y se obtiene un cuadrado. Nótese lo que no hay en este razonamiento: ningún detalle sobre la naturaleza de la atracción. Solo se necesita que exista y que actúe a distancias cortas.
steps.figCaption: En el interior del gas, la atracción de los vecinos se anula en todas direcciones; cerca de la pared, los vecinos quedan solo detrás, y la molécula golpea con menos fuerza

steps.text: Juntamos todo. En la ecuación del gas ideal, reemplazamos el volumen por el libre, y a la presión medida le sumamos lo que la atracción quitó: obtenemos la ecuación de Van der Waals. Verifiquémosla de tres maneras. Dimensiones: $[b] = $ m³/mol, para que $nb$ sea un volumen; $[a] = $ Pa·m⁶/mol², para que $an^2/V^2$ sea una presión. Límite: cuando $V \to \infty$, ambas correcciones desaparecen y queda exactamente $pV = nRT$, como debe ser para un gas enrarecido. Orden de magnitud en condiciones normales (un mol ocupa 22,41 litros): $nb/V = 42{,}7/22\,410 = 0{,}19\,\%$, y $an^2/V^2 = 0{,}3640/0{,}02241^{2} = 725$ Pa, es decir, 0,72 por ciento de una atmósfera. Ambas correcciones son menores del uno por ciento: por eso el gas ideal satisfizo a todos durante tanto tiempo y sigue satisfaciendo en la mayoría de los cálculos.
steps.figCaption: Las dos correcciones en su lugar: a la presión se le suma lo que la atracción quitó, del volumen se resta lo que ocuparon las propias moléculas

steps.text: Ahora veamos qué dice la ecuación sobre la forma de las isotermas. Fijemos $T$ y resolvamos la ecuación para $V$: después de multiplicar por $V^{2}$, resulta ser cúbica, y por lo tanto a una presión dada puede tener una o tres raíces. Esto ya es una pista. A alta temperatura, la curva $p(V)$ es monótonamente decreciente y casi indistinguible de la hipérbola del gas ideal. A baja temperatura aparece una joroba: una región donde la presión aumenta con el volumen. Físicamente esto es imposible, y no es imposible "porque es extraño", sino por una razón concreta. Supongamos que en ese medio surge accidentalmente una condensación. Un volumen reducido significa aquí una presión reducida, la materia vecina se precipita hacia adentro, la condensación crece, la presión cae aún más. No hay fuerza restauradora en ninguna etapa: el estado es mecánicamente inestable y simplemente no se realiza.
steps.latex: pV^{3} - (pb + RT)\,V^{2} + aV - ab = 0 \qquad (n = 1), \qquad \text{prohibido: } \left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial V}\right)_T > 0
steps.figCaption: Tres isotermas: por encima de la temperatura crítica la curva es monótona, por debajo tiene una joroba, y la región con presión creciente al aumentar el volumen es mecánicamente imposible

steps.text: ¿Qué hay realmente allí? El experimento de Andrews responde: en lugar de la joroba, hay una meseta estrictamente horizontal. Mientras dura la meseta, la compresión no cambia la presión en absoluto; cambia otra cosa: la proporción de líquido aumenta, la de vapor disminuye, y en un extremo de la meseta la sustancia es todo vapor, en el otro todo líquido. La altura de la meseta, sin embargo, no puede ser cualquiera. Maxwell notó que si se la traza en el lugar equivocado, entonces, yendo por la meseta en una dirección y por la curva de Van der Waals de regreso, volveríamos al estado inicial habiendo obtenido un trabajo no nulo a una sola temperatura. Eso no ocurre. Por lo tanto, el trabajo en un camino cerrado es cero, y esto significa exactamente que la meseta corta de la joroba y del valle áreas iguales.
steps.figCaption: Regla de las áreas iguales de Maxwell: la horizontal se traza de modo que las áreas sombreadas por encima y por debajo coincidan; solo entonces el trabajo en un camino cerrado es cero

steps.text: Cuanto mayor es la temperatura, más corta es la meseta: el líquido y el vapor se diferencian cada vez menos. A cierta temperatura, la joroba y el valle se fusionan en un solo punto, la meseta se contrae a cero y la diferencia entre líquido y vapor desaparece por completo. Matemáticamente, en este punto la tangente es horizontal y simultáneamente la curva cambia el signo de la curvatura, es decir, se anulan a la vez la primera y la segunda derivada de la presión con respecto al volumen a temperatura constante. La primera condición da $RT/(V-b)^{2} = 2a/V^{3}$, la segunda da $RT/(V-b)^{3} = 3a/V^{4}$. Dividiendo la primera por la segunda, obtenemos $V - b = 2V/3$, es decir, $V_c = 3b$; sustituyendo esto en la primera condición, encontramos $RT_c = 8a/(27b)$, y sustituyendo ambas en la propia ecuación de estado, $p_c = a/(27b^{2})$. Ahora los números. Para el dióxido de carbono ($a = 3{,}640$ l²·bar/mol², $b = 42{,}67$ cm³/mol) resulta 304,0 K y 74,0 bar frente a los medidos 304,13 K y 73,77 bar: un error del 0,04 y 0,4 por ciento. Para el agua ($a = 5{,}536$, $b = 30{,}49$) resulta 647,0 K y 220,6 bar frente a 647,10 K y 220,64 bar, es decir, los mismos 374 °C y 218 atmósferas que en el tema de las transiciones de fase se denominan límite de aplicabilidad de la curva de ebullición. Para el nitrógeno, 126,2 K y 33,9 bar frente a 126,2 y 34,0; para el helio, 5,18 K y 2,26 bar frente a 5,19 y 2,27. Cuatro sustancias, una dispersión de temperaturas críticas de ciento veinte veces, un error de fracciones de porcentaje.
steps.latex: \left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial V}\right)_T = -\frac{RT}{(V-b)^{2}} + \frac{2a}{V^{3}} = 0, \quad \left(\frac{\partial^{2} p}{\partial V^{2}}\right)_T = \frac{2RT}{(V-b)^{3}} - \frac{6a}{V^{4}} = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; V_c = 3b,\ \ T_c = \frac{8a}{27Rb},\ \ p_c = \frac{a}{27b^{2}}
steps.figCaption: El punto crítico es el lugar donde el máximo y el mínimo de la isoterma se fusionan: la tangente es horizontal y, simultáneamente, la curvatura cambia de signo, y de estas dos condiciones se obtienen las tres coordenadas

steps.text: Queda la consecuencia principal y la verificación honesta principal. Por encima de la temperatura crítica, la ecuación cúbica tiene exactamente una raíz a cualquier presión: no hay meseta, no hay coexistencia, no se forma menisco. Comprima todo lo que quiera: la sustancia se espesará gradualmente hasta volverse más densa que el agua, pero nunca verá una interfaz de fases. Esto es exactamente lo que significa que por encima de $T_c$ el gas no se puede licuar por ninguna presión, y esto es lo que Andrews vio en el dióxido de carbono por encima de 31 °C. Y la verificación es esta. Formemos a partir de las tres coordenadas críticas la combinación adimensional $Z_c = p_cV_c/(RT_c)$. Las constantes $a$ y $b$ se cancelan por completo, y queda un número puro $3/8 = 0{,}375$, el mismo para todas las sustancias del mundo. Esto ya no es un ajuste, sino una predicción, y solo se puede confirmar o refutar. Experimento: 0,274 para el dióxido de carbono, 0,229 para el agua, 0,289 para el nitrógeno, 0,301 para el helio. Ninguno es igual a 0,375. El modelo falla por un tercio, y el fallo está enteramente en el volumen: $V_c = 3b$ da para el CO$_2$ 128 cm³/mol frente a los 94 medidos.
steps.figCaption: Por encima de la temperatura crítica no hay meseta a ninguna presión: la sustancia se espesa continuamente y la frontera entre líquido y gas no aparece en absoluto

derivation.plateCap: Dos correcciones al gas ideal y ninguna más. A la izquierda, entre paréntesis, la presión que habría si las moléculas no se atrajeran; a la derecha, entre paréntesis, el volumen que les queda para moverse. Toda la recompensa inesperada —isotermas con joroba, meseta de coexistencia, punto crítico y ley de los estados correspondientes— se obtiene de estas dos correcciones y dos derivadas.
derivation.note: Enumeremos lo que hemos supuesto en el camino. Primero: las moléculas son esferas rígidas. El potencial repulsivo real no es una pared vertical, sino una pendiente pronunciada, y el "diámetro" de la molécula depende por tanto de la energía con la que se la golpea, es decir, de la temperatura. Segundo, y esto es más pesado: reemplazamos la atracción por un promedio. Cada molécula siente no a vecinos concretos, sino un campo uniforme creado por la densidad media. Esta aproximación se llama aproximación de campo medio, y se derrumba precisamente donde es más interesante: cerca del punto crítico, donde la densidad fluctúa en grandes manchas. Tercero: $a$ y $b$ se consideran constantes, independientes de la temperatura y de la densidad. Cuarto: no hemos distinguido en ningún lugar entre diferentes moléculas, es decir, la ecuación está escrita para una sustancia pura, no para una mezcla. Quinto: la regla de las áreas iguales no la hemos demostrado, sino que la hemos justificado con el razonamiento del trabajo en un camino cerrado; la demostración rigurosa pasa por la igualdad de los potenciales químicos de las fases y pertenece a la termodinámica de Gibbs. Finalmente, conviene llamar a las cosas por su nombre: no estamos ante una derivación desde primeros principios, sino ante una corrección de una ecuación conocida con dos términos razonables. Su valor no está en la precisión —la precisión, como hemos visto, es mediocre—, sino en que a partir de casi nada predice la existencia del punto crítico, que antes nadie sabía explicar.

math.title: Matemáticas que aquí se necesitaron
math.lead: Tres temas: cómo estimar, qué corrección es ahora la principal, por qué la derivada necesita un subíndice, y cómo la integral fija de manera inequívoca la altura de la plataforma.

items.what: Qué corrección gana: estimación de órdenes
items.why: Hay dos correcciones, y tiran de $Z$ en direcciones opuestas: el volumen propio hace que $Z$ sea mayor que uno, la atracción lo hace menor. Quién gana se ve a partir de la expansión en baja densidad. Expandimos la ecuación en potencias de $1/V_m$ y nos quedamos con el primer término: $Z \approx 1 + (b - a/RT)/V_m$. Todo lo decide el paréntesis. Si $a/RT > b$, es decir, a bajas temperaturas, gana la atracción y $Z < 1$ — exactamente lo que vimos con el dióxido de carbono. Si la temperatura es alta, el paréntesis es positivo y el gas es "más rígido" que el ideal. Justo en el límite, a $T = a/(Rb)$, las correcciones se cancelan mutuamente, y el gas real en un amplio rango de presiones es indistinguible del ideal: esta temperatura se llama temperatura de Boyle. Para van der Waals es igual a $\tfrac{27}{8}T_c$, es decir, 1026 K para CO$_2$ y 426 K para el nitrógeno, mientras que los valores medidos son alrededor de 714 y 327 K. La sobreestimación de un tercio para el nitrógeno y de casi una vez y media para el dióxido de carbono es el mismo orden de inexactitud que el de $Z_c$, y esto no es coincidencia: ambas cantidades prueban el modelo donde ya no es cuantitativo.

En la condición del punto crítico no aparece $dp/dV$, sino $(\partial p/\partial V)_T$, y el subíndice aquí es esencial, no un adorno. La presión depende de dos variables a la vez, y "la derivada con respecto al volumen" sin especificar qué se hace con la segunda variable simplemente no está definida: a lo largo de una isoterma se obtiene un número, a lo largo de una adiabática otro, y a lo largo de una isocora la pregunta no tiene sentido. Fijamos la temperatura porque la isoterma es exactamente lo que dibuja el experimento de Andrews. Luego conviene contar las ecuaciones y las incógnitas. Hay tres incógnitas: $V_c$, $T_c$, $p_c$. También hay tres ecuaciones: la propia ecuación de estado más dos condiciones sobre las derivadas. El sistema está cerrado, y por eso el punto crítico se obtiene de manera única, sin necesidad de conocimiento adicional sobre la sustancia.
items.latex: \left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial V}\right)_T = 0, \qquad \left(\frac{\partial^{2} p}{\partial V^{2}}\right)_T = 0, \qquad p = p(V_c, T_c)

items.what: La integral que pone la plataforma en su lugar
items.why: La regla de las áreas iguales parece geométrica, pero se calcula analíticamente, y para van der Waals la integral se resuelve completamente en funciones elementales. Necesitamos $\int p\,dV$ a lo largo de la isoterma; el primer término da un logaritmo, el segundo da uno sobre el volumen. Al igualar el área bajo la línea recta de la plataforma con el área bajo la curva, obtenemos una ecuación que relaciona la presión de saturación con los dos volúmenes. Otras dos ecuaciones dan las igualdades $p(V_l) = p(V_g) = p_{\text{nas}}$. Tres ecuaciones, tres incógnitas — el problema se resuelve numéricamente, y esto es exactamente lo que hace el simulador cuando dibuja la cúpula de coexistencia. Es útil notar que la misma integral es el trabajo: la igualdad de áreas significa trabajo cero en un camino isotérmico cerrado, y un trabajo no nulo implicaría una máquina que extrae trabajo de un solo reservorio térmico.
items.latex: \int p\,dV = RT\ln(V-b) + \frac{a}{V} \;\Longrightarrow\; p_{\text{nas}}(V_g - V_l) = RT\ln\frac{V_g - b}{V_l - b} + \frac{a}{V_g} - \frac{a}{V_l}

example.title: Ejemplo con números
example.lead: Calculemos el punto crítico del dióxido de carbono a partir de dos constantes tabuladas y verifiquemos la respuesta con un extintor rojo que se encuentra en cualquier pasillo.
example.given: Para el dióxido de carbono $a = 3{,}640$ l²·bar/mol², $b = 0{,}04267$ l/mol. La constante de los gases en estas unidades es $R = 0{,}083145$ l·bar/(mol·K). Hallar $T_c$, $p_c$, $V_c$ y la relación adimensional $Z_c$; comparar con los valores medidos 304,13 K, 73,8 bar y 94 cm³/mol.
example.law: $V_c = 3b$, $T_c = 8a/(27Rb)$, $p_c = a/(27b^{2})$ — tres fórmulas obtenidas de la condición de fusión del máximo y el mínimo de la isoterma.

solution.text: Temperatura. En el denominador hay un producto de tres números; lo calculamos primero para no perder el orden de magnitud.
Presión. Aquí $b$ está al cuadrado, por lo que el error en $b$ entra duplicado; conviene recordarlo al hacer estimaciones.
Volumen: la fórmula más simple y, como veremos, la más desafortunada.
Verificación adimensional. La calculamos de dos maneras: mediante la fórmula $3/8$ y sustituyendo los valores medidos. La discrepancia es el precio del modelo.

Reunimos los errores y vemos dónde reside exactamente la discrepancia. La temperatura falla por un 0,04 por ciento, la presión por un 0,4, el volumen por un 36. La relación $0{,}375/0{,}274 = 1{,}37$ coincide con la relación $128{,}1/94 = 1{,}36$: toda la inexactitud de $Z_c$ es la inexactitud de $V_c$, y nada más.

example.answer: Punto crítico del dióxido de carbono: 304 K, es decir, 31 °C, a 74 bares. La temperatura y la presión se predicen con precisión de fracciones de porcentaje; el volumen crítico está sobreestimado en un tercio.
example.check: ¿Es razonable y qué se sigue de ello? Treinta y un grados es temperatura ambiente, y he aquí una consecuencia directa. En un extintor a 20 °C, es decir, por debajo de la crítica, el dióxido de carbono se encuentra en la meseta de coexistencia: en su interior hay líquido y vapor, la presión es de 57 bares y no depende de cuánta sustancia quede; por eso no hay manómetro en un extintor de CO2, se pesa. Comprobemos la masa. La densidad del dióxido de carbono líquido a 20 °C es de unos 0,77 kg por litro, y la norma de llenado de los cilindros es de 0,75 kg por litro. Es decir, el cilindro se llena de líquido casi hasta arriba, dejando solo unos pocos por ciento para la expansión, y tal escasez de reserva exige una explicación: significa que calentar el cilindro está terminantemente prohibido. Saque el mismo extintor al sol y el desastre llegará antes del punto crítico. La densidad de carga de 0,75 kg/l es superior a la densidad crítica del dióxido de carbono, que se calcula a partir del $V_c$ ya obtenido: 44 g/mol dividido por 94 cm³/mol da 0,47 kg/l. Por tanto, al calentar no desaparecerá el líquido, sino el vapor: el líquido se expande, devora la burbuja de vapor y ya alrededor de 22 °C llena el cilindro por completo. A partir de ahí no tiene dónde expandirse, las paredes son rígidas y el líquido es casi incompresible: la presión no aumenta en porcentajes, sino en múltiplos, mucho antes de que el termómetro llegue a 31 °C. Por eso el cilindro lleva una membrana de ruptura y debe almacenarse en un lugar fresco. La segunda consecuencia se comprueba en sentido contrario: para el oxígeno y el nitrógeno, las temperaturas críticas son 155 y 126 K, muy por debajo de la ambiente, y en los cilindros siempre son gas, por mucho que se comprima. Si su cálculo dio para el dióxido de carbono una temperatura crítica de cien kelvins o de mil, busque el 27 perdido en el denominador o los grados Celsius en lugar de kelvins.

constants.title: Constantes de esta sección
constants.lead: Cinco números: una constante universal, dos constantes tabuladas de sustancias, un punto crítico de importancia práctica y un número adimensional que revela las imprecisiones del modelo.

items.name: Constante universal de los gases
items.why: Desde 2019 no se mide, sino que se calcula exactamente: $R = N_A k_B$, y ambas cantidades están definidas como números fijos según la nueva definición del SI. En los cálculos de gases reales también son convenientes otras unidades: 0,083145 L·bar/(mol·K) — así los volúmenes se expresan en litros y las presiones en bares, y en las fórmulas del punto crítico no hay que lidiar con potencias de diez.
items.mnemo: Ocho y tres décimas. De aquí se obtiene directamente el volumen molar en condiciones normales: $22{,}4 = 8{,}314\cdot 273/101\,325\cdot 1000$ litros.

items.name: Constante de atracción del dióxido de carbono
items.why: Es una medida de cuán fuertemente se atraen las moléculas entre sí, y su variación entre sustancias es enorme: para el helio es 0,00346, para el nitrógeno 0,1370, para el dióxido de carbono 0,3640, para el agua 0,5536 — un factor de ciento sesenta de un extremo a otro. El orden de esta serie se lee directamente: un átomo inerte solitario, una molécula no polar, una molécula con un fuerte momento cuadrupolar, una molécula con enlaces de hidrógeno. Precisamente $a$ es responsable de que el agua sea líquida a temperatura ambiente, mientras que el nitrógeno a la misma temperatura es gas.
items.mnemo: Mire $a$ como la temperatura de licuefacción: $T_c = 8a/(27Rb)$, y como $b$ es del mismo orden para todas las sustancias, la temperatura crítica es casi proporcional a $a$.

items.name: Constante de volumen propio del dióxido de carbono
items.why: La variación aquí es incomparablemente menor que la de $a$: helio 23,8, agua 30,5, nitrógeno 38,7, dióxido de carbono 42,7 cm³/mol — solo un factor de dos de un extremo a otro, porque todas las moléculas tienen aproximadamente el mismo tamaño, y el tamaño entra al cubo. Una lectura útil de este número: 42,7 cm³/mol es cuatro veces el volumen total de las propias moléculas, por lo que el volumen propio de un mol de dióxido de carbono es de unos 10,7 cm³. Compárese con los 22 400 cm³ que ocupa un mol de gas: las moléculas llenan el cinco centésimas por ciento del espacio que se les ofrece.
items.mnemo: $b$ es aproximadamente igual al volumen molar de la sustancia en estado líquido: para el dióxido de carbono, el líquido da 57 cm³/mol a 20 °C — el mismo orden. Esto no es casualidad: en el líquido, las moléculas están justamente apretadas.

items.name: Punto crítico del agua
items.why: El número alrededor del cual se construye toda la termoenergética. Una caldera de vapor convencional opera con un tambor donde el agua hirviendo se separa del vapor — pero por encima del punto crítico no existe la ebullición, no hay nada que separar, y el tambor no es necesario en absoluto. Las centrales supercríticas funcionan a 24–25 MPa y 540–600 °C, las ultrasupercríticas a 30 MPa y más. La ganancia es directa: cuanto mayor es la temperatura del fluido de trabajo, mayor es el rendimiento máximo, y el paso a través del punto crítico elevó el rendimiento de las centrales de carbón de aproximadamente 38 a 45 por ciento. En el tema de transiciones de fase, este mismo punto se denomina el límite más allá del cual la curva de ebullición simplemente termina.
items.mnemo: 374 grados y 218 atmósferas. Recuerde como «doscientas veces la presión atmosférica y el doble de caliente que el agua hirviendo» — ambas mitades son fáciles de recordar.

items.name: Coeficiente de compresibilidad crítico
items.value: 3/8 = 0,375 según Van der Waals; 0,229 para el agua, 0,274 para el CO₂, 0,289 para el nitrógeno, 0,301 para el helio
items.why: La ausencia de unidades no es un detalle menor, sino todo el contenido. Al ser adimensional, $a$ y $b$ se cancelan, es decir, toda la información sobre la sustancia específica desaparece; queda una predicción pura del modelo que no se puede ajustar. Los experimentos dan números notablemente menores que 3/8. La dispersión entre sustancias también es real, pero pequeña en comparación con la dispersión de las constantes: $Z_c$ varía de 0,23 a 0,30, es decir, en un tercio, mientras que las propias $a$ varían en un factor de ciento sesenta. Ecuaciones de estado posteriores corrigieron precisamente este indicador: Redlich y Kwong en 1949 obtuvieron 1/3, Peng y Robinson en 1976 obtuvieron 0,307, que ya se acerca a lo medido.
items.mnemo: Tres octavos es el único número en toda la sección que no depende ni de la sustancia ni de las unidades. Por eso sirve como veredicto del modelo.

synthesis.title: Cómo se relaciona con el resto del curso
synthesis.lead: Este párrafo se sitúa exactamente entre dos grandes temas: toma el gas ideal y lo rompe con dos correcciones, y la ruptura resultante explica lo que en termodinámica hasta ahora se tomaba de la experiencia.

items.text: La ecuación $pV = nRT$ se deriva en el tema sobre la estructura molecular a partir de los impactos de moléculas puntuales contra la pared, y allí también se ve lo que falta en esa derivación: el tamaño de las moléculas y la fuerza entre ellas. Hemos devuelto ambos y a cambio hemos obtenido el punto crítico. Nótese la dirección de la dependencia: el gas real no es una "ley diferente", sino la misma con dos adiciones, y cuando $V \to \infty$ las adiciones desaparecen. Así está construida casi toda extensión de una teoría: lo nuevo debe contener lo viejo como caso límite.

items.h: Transiciones de fase: a lo que hemos dado fundamento
items.text: En el tema de las transiciones de fase, la curva de ebullición y la ecuación de Clausius-Clapeyron describen el equilibrio entre líquido y vapor, pero la existencia misma de tal equilibrio se acepta allí como un dato de la experiencia. Aquí ha surgido: la meseta en la isoterma es la coexistencia de fases, y sus extremos son las densidades del líquido y del vapor saturado. Allí mismo, el punto crítico del agua se llamó el límite donde la curva de ebullición se interrumpe, y ahora se entiende por qué: los extremos de la meseta convergen, la diferencia entre fases desaparece, no hay entre qué pasar el límite.

items.h: Estadística: qué atrae a las moléculas
items.text: La corrección $a$ no dice nada sobre el origen de la atracción; le basta con que exista. Ese origen se analiza en la física estadística: incluso en moléculas neutras no polares, las fluctuaciones instantáneas de la nube electrónica inducen un dipolo en la vecina, y surge una atracción que decae como la sexta potencia de la distancia. Estas fuerzas llevan el nombre de Van der Waals, por la misma ecuación, y no al revés. De allí también viene la explicación de por qué a alta temperatura la atracción deja de molestar: la energía del movimiento térmico supera la energía de atracción, y las moléculas se separan sin llegar a unirse.

El segundo párrafo se ocupará de la superficie. Esa misma fuerza que aquí hemos condensado en una constante $a$, en el límite del líquido no está compensada, y de ahí surgen la tensión superficial, las gotas, los meniscos y la ascensión del agua en los capilares. Por cierto, queda claro por qué la tensión superficial se anula en el punto crítico: allí desaparece la propia frontera entre fases, y con ella su costo. El tercer párrafo tratará las capacidades caloríficas y mostrará que para un gas real la relación habitual $C_p - C_V = R$ deja de ser exacta: las mismas dos correcciones son las culpables.

items.h: Licuefacción de gases: dónde funciona esto
items.text: La temperatura crítica es lo primero que mira un ingeniero criogénico. El dióxido de carbono a temperatura ambiente se licúa por simple compresión; el aire, no, y ningún compresor ayudará: primero hay que enfriarlo por debajo de 132 K. Se enfría mediante la estrangulación de Joule-Thomson, es decir, la expansión del gas comprimido a través de un orificio estrecho; funciona precisamente gracias a la corrección $a$ y por eso es imposible para un gas ideal. La derivación de este efecto no cabe en nuestro párrafo, y lo presentamos aquí como un hecho. Por esta misma escalera se descendió históricamente: el aire en 1895, el hidrógeno en 1898, el helio en 1908, y cada gas siguiente requería que el anterior lo enfriara previamente.

curiosities.title: Curiosidades: compruébelo con sus manos
curiosities.lead: Ambas correcciones de Van der Waals se pueden comprobar en la cocina en cinco minutos, y literalmente: una se siente con la palma de la mano, la otra se ve a través del plástico.
